conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: s0B
candidates.idea: Combine P's first-viewport access to the name and three code columns with R's narrower link column. This should retain P's lookup advantage while reducing total scroll distance, at the cost of a wrapped link header and long country name.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Country names and codes are easy to scan, and the initial viewport contains the name and three code columns. The ISO link heading wraps naturally; its column and independence require scrolling.
Names and codes are easy to scan, and the first four columns fit together in the initial view. The remaining columns require scrolling, and the wrapped headers make the header row tall.
The compact rows preserve names and identifiers, and the first view contains the name and three code columns. The link header wraps naturally, and the final two columns require scrolling.

candidates.name: d2r4B
candidates.idea: Test a viewport-fitting allocation that protects Afghanistan, three-character alpha codes, numeric codes, and Yes while accepting fragmented headers and wrapped links. The widths sum to 359 px.
candidates.label: bad

whys: The country names and short codes remain mostly legible within the viewport, but headings split into fragments and ISO identifiers break over several lines, making rows tall and difficult to compare.
All columns are visible and country names mostly remain whole, but headers break within words and link identifiers fragment across several lines. Tall rows make scanning slow.

Country names and short codes are mostly easy to find, but several headers fragment into small pieces and link identifiers split across three or four lines. Tall rows and scattered fragments impede comparison.

candidates.name: d1r1A
candidates.idea: Test a compact scrolling layout: allow long multiword names to wrap, keep Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 intact, and widen the link column enough for all links on one line. The first four columns total 360px, bringing the three code columns into the initial viewport.
candidates.label: gold

whys: The first viewport has the same useful coverage as A, and the ISO link heading stays on one line. The extra width slightly increases the distance to the independence column without changing the row heights.
The initial view keeps names and all three code columns together. The link header stays on one line, although its extra width adds scrolling without reducing the table's height.

Names and identifiers stay intact, the link header fits on one line, and the first view includes the name and three code columns. The two rightmost columns require scrolling; the wider link column adds some horizontal travel.

candidates.name: d3r4A
candidates.idea: Test a modestly wider name column to keep American Samoa on one line while retaining intact references. The first viewport would cut slightly into the numeric column, so compare that cost against the shorter rows in d3r1B.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Names and codes scan cleanly, with compact, mostly uniform rows. The wider name column improves its heading break, but the numeric heading reaches the viewport edge and the last two columns require scrolling.
Names and codes remain legible with compact, mostly uniform rows. The wider name column does not reduce wrapping in the body and leaves the numeric column edge beyond the initial viewport.

Names and identifiers are intact, and the first view includes the name and three code columns. The first header leaves ‘case)’ isolated on its last line, and the final two columns require horizontal scrolling.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Equal columns ignore the different lengths and roles of the content: country names and link identifiers would break severely, while short code columns receive space they do not need.
candidates.label: bad

whys: Country names, headings and link identifiers fragment across many lines. The very tall header and rows make lookup laborious, despite the table being only one pixel wider than the viewport.
Equal columns split country names, headers and link identifiers repeatedly. The very tall header and rows make lookup laborious, while the table still exceeds the viewport slightly.

Like B, the equal narrow columns fragment country names, headings and link identifiers. The tall header and rows are difficult to scan, while the one-pixel overflow brings no meaningful reading benefit.
Names and short codes are readable, but every ISO identifier wraps across three lines, making every row tall. The initial viewport also cuts through the link column, so it needs scrolling to read.

Country names and short codes are readable, but every link identifier wraps across three lines, making every body row tall. The initial viewport cuts through the link column and hides the independence column.
Names and short codes remain legible, but each link identifier occupies three lines and makes every data row tall. The viewport cuts through the link column, while independence is offscreen.
Equal narrow columns split country names, headings and identifiers repeatedly. The oversized header and tall rows severely hinder scanning, even though all columns fit.
The table fits, but country names, headings and link identifiers break into fragments throughout. The towering header and sparse, tall rows severely hinder lookup and comparison.
All columns fit, but country names, headings and link identifiers break repeatedly within words or codes. The extremely tall header and rows make scanning and lookup laborious.

d1.purpose: Provide a reference for finding the current ISO 3166-1 codes and independence status of each listed country or territory.
tasks: Find a country or territory by name and read across its row to retrieve a code or status.
Compare alpha-2, alpha-3 or numeric codes down a column, preserving leading zeros.
Use the ISO 3166-2 link associated with a country or territory.
Scan the alphabetical list sequentially and distinguish independent from non-independent entries.
relations: Each row binds one name to its alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric identifiers, subdivision link and independence status.
The alpha-2 code also appears at the end of the corresponding ISO 3166-2 link.
The three code columns are parallel identifiers, while the link and independence columns provide related information.
roles: The first column identifies the row and anchors lookup, even though no row headers are declared.
The three code columns support precise lookup and comparison.
The link column points to subdivision codes; the final column records a binary status.
Column headers distinguish similar identifiers and must remain understandable when wrapped.
keep_whole: Alpha-2 and alpha-3 codes and three-digit numeric codes, including leading zeros.
ISO 3166-2 link identifiers, where available width permits.
Individual words in names and headers, especially Independent, where available width permits.
may_wrap: Multiword country and territory names at spaces.
Headers between words, keeping Alpha-2, Alpha-3 and ISO 3166-2 recognizable.
same_scale: Alpha-2 and alpha-3 columns should have similar widths because their roles and content lengths are similar.
The numeric code column can be comparable in scale to the alpha columns; the name and link columns need more room for longer content.
d1.h_vs_v: A 359px table forces some words or identifiers to split and increases row height, but keeps all columns in the initial view. A wider table preserves semantic units and reduces vertical disruption, while requiring horizontal scrolling and making it harder to keep the name visible alongside rightmost values.

d2.purpose: Provide a reference for looking up current ISO 3166-1 codes and related information by country or territory.
tasks: Find a country or territory by its English short name.
Read and compare its alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric codes.
Locate its ISO 3166-2 link and independence status.
relations: Each row connects one country or territory to its codes, link and status.
The alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric codes are parallel identifiers; the ISO 3166-2 link incorporates the alpha-2 code.
roles: The first column identifies each record, although no row headers are declared.
The next three columns contain compact codes; the fifth contains a longer link; the sixth contains a short status.
Column headers explain the meaning of the values and may need more space than the values themselves.
keep_whole: Alpha codes and three-digit numeric codes, including leading zeros.
Individual words in country names and headers wherever space permits.
may_wrap: In a viewport-fitting layout, some long words and identifiers must split.
same_scale: The alpha-2 and alpha-3 columns should have similar widths because their values and headers have parallel roles.
The numeric code column can be close in scale to the alpha columns.
The country-name and link columns need more room than the compact code columns.
d2.h_vs_v: A fitted table exposes all columns at once but forces disruptive breaks and taller rows. Scrolling preserves identifiers and makes rows easier to scan, at the cost of moving horizontally to see the link and status.

d3.purpose: Provide a reference for the first 14 current ISO 3166-1 entries and their associated codes, subdivision links and independence status.
tasks: Find an entry by its English name.
Read or compare its alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric codes.
Locate its ISO 3166-2 link and independence status.
relations: Each row describes one country or territory; its codes, subdivision link and status belong together.
The two alphabetic codes and the numeric code are parallel identifiers.
The ISO 3166-2 link incorporates the entry's alpha-2 code.
roles: The header names each field; the first column acts as the visual row label even though no row headers are declared.
The remaining columns contain compact identifiers, a reference link and a short categorical status.
All 14 body rows have the same structural role.
keep_whole: Country and territory names should retain whole words where space permits.
Alpha codes and three-digit numeric codes, including leading zeroes, must remain intact.
ISO 3166-2 references should ideally stay intact because they are identifiers.
Header words should remain whole where feasible.
may_wrap: Multiword names can wrap between words.
Headers can wrap between words and at natural punctuation; narrow fitted columns may force breaks within header words or references.
same_scale: Alpha-2 and alpha-3 columns should have similar widths because they hold parallel short codes.
Body rows share one visual hierarchy; the name column deserves more space because its entries are longer.
d3.h_vs_v: A fitted table exposes all fields at once but forces awkward breaks, especially in headers and links, and increases row heights. Scrolling preserves identifiers and compact rows, but readers must move horizontally to see later fields and may lose the name from view.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport contains the names and all three code columns. Body identifiers remain intact, and most rows are compact.
analysis.faults: The long name wraps, the first header takes three lines, and the alpha headers split their labels at the hyphen. The link and independence columns require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: It prioritizes the four lookup columns within the initial viewport, while giving the link and independence columns enough room to remain on one line.

analysis.strengths: Every body row is one line high, country names read continuously, and the headers fit within two lines. Its even row rhythm makes scanning easy.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through the numeric column, so only the name and two alpha codes are fully visible. It also requires the most horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: It spends extra width on the name and alpha columns to reduce wrapping and create a uniform, compact table.

analysis.strengths: Like P, it keeps names and all three code columns essentially within the first viewport and preserves body identifiers. It is the narrowest scrolling layout shown.
analysis.faults: The long name wraps, the first header takes three lines, and the link header wraps as well. The numeric column ends at the viewport edge, leaving little tolerance for any difference in available width.
analysis.spatial_logic: It trades some link-column width for a slightly wider name column and a shorter overall scroll distance.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible together, and the short alpha codes, numeric codes, and Yes/No values remain whole.
analysis.faults: Headers break repeatedly inside words, and link identifiers are fragmented across several lines. Tall, uneven rows make cross-column lookup slow and weaken visual order.
analysis.spatial_logic: It distributes the viewport among all six columns, protecting the name and short values at the cost of severely compressed headers and links.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible together, and most rows have a consistent height. The slightly wider link column reduces some link wrapping.
analysis.faults: Numeric codes and Yes values split across lines, in addition to the fragmented headers and links. This damages the very identifiers the table is meant to support.
analysis.spatial_logic: It moves a few pixels toward the alpha and link columns, but takes them from the numeric and independence columns, crossing thresholds needed to keep their values whole.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve the table's identifiers and reading flow much better. P favors immediate access to three code columns; Q favors whole names and uniform rows. In the fitted class, small width changes matter: S preserves short values that T breaks, even though S is taller. A fitted design must still accept substantial header and link fragmentation at this font size.

analysis.strengths: All names and identifiers stay on one line, with compact, uniform body rows and no measured word breaks. The first viewport shows the name and both alphabetic codes clearly.
analysis.faults: The numeric header is cut by the viewport edge, and the link and independence columns require scrolling. The alpha headers split after the hyphen.
analysis.spatial_logic: A generous name column supports scanning while narrow code columns keep the full table relatively compact.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport contains the name and all three code columns, with identifiers intact. The full table is narrower than s0A.
analysis.faults: The name header takes three lines and Antigua and Barbuda wraps, interrupting otherwise uniform rows. The link and independence columns begin off screen.
analysis.spatial_logic: Trading name-column width for a complete numeric column at first sight favors code lookup over a compact vertical rhythm.

analysis.strengths: Nearly all columns are visible at once, and the ISO 3166-2 links wrap consistently in three lines.
analysis.faults: Headers fragment severely, several alphabetic codes split across lines, and the table is very tall. It also overflows the viewport by one pixel.
analysis.spatial_logic: Compressing every column produces narrow vertical strips and large row heights, making comparison harder despite the broad initial view.

analysis.strengths: Like s0B, it shows names and all three codes at first sight with identifiers intact. The link header fits on one line.
analysis.faults: The three-line name header and wrapped Antigua and Barbuda row remain. The wider link column increases scrolling without improving the first viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: Extra width is spent on a secondary header while the tighter name column determines the table height.

analysis.strengths: Names and identifiers remain intact, body rows are uniformly compact, and alpha headers keep Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 together.
analysis.faults: The numeric codes are cut at the first viewport edge, and the table is the widest of the scrolling options.
analysis.spatial_logic: Generous header and name widths make the full table orderly but reduce the useful information visible before scrolling.

analysis.strengths: It fits the viewport and keeps the standalone alpha and numeric codes intact.
analysis.faults: Headers fragment heavily, many link identifiers split within their suffixes, and variable, very tall rows make comparison laborious.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width shifted toward the alpha-code columns protects their values, but the squeezed link column drives the greatest height and uneven rhythm.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve codes and make row comparisons much easier. s0B and P expose all three code columns initially, while s0A and Q give names a more compact rhythm. In the fitting layouts, protecting standalone codes consumes width needed by the link identifiers and headers; fitting all six columns comes at a substantial readability cost.

analysis.strengths: Country names, codes and links are readable, with no measured breaks inside words. The first viewport includes all four lookup columns.
analysis.faults: The Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 headers each break across three lines, separating the hyphenated labels awkwardly. Antigua and Barbuda takes two lines, and the link and independence columns require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The compact first four columns make good use of the initial viewport, but the three-line header creates a tall band above mostly single-line rows.

analysis.strengths: All six columns are visible at once, and the numeric and alpha-code values remain readily comparable.
analysis.faults: The independence header is broken almost letter by letter, Yes and No split, and the ISO links wrap into three fragments. The resulting tall header and rows make lookup laborious.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow last column saves horizontal space at the cost of a disproportionately tall header and fragmented repeated values.

analysis.strengths: All country names and data values fit on one line, and the headers wrap naturally into at most two lines. Uniform row heights make scanning especially easy.
analysis.faults: The first viewport cuts through the numeric column, including its header; the link and independence columns are also offscreen. It requires the most horizontal scrolling of these candidates.
analysis.spatial_logic: Extra width in the name column produces a compact, regular table, but shifts part of an important lookup column beyond the initial view.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport includes names and all three code columns. Alpha headers wrap more naturally than in s1B, and the body retains intact codes and links.
analysis.faults: The name header needs three lines, and Antigua and Barbuda wraps to two. The link and independence columns require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A narrower name column trades a little vertical regularity for a useful initial view of the four primary lookup columns.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible, Yes and No remain whole, and the header is much shorter than in s1C.
analysis.faults: Several headers break inside words, while some ISO links split their final country code across lines. Variable row heights and fragmented identifiers slow comparison.
analysis.spatial_logic: Moving width from the link column to the independence column improves the latter but creates repeated four-line link cells and uneven row rhythm.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve the identifiers and a usable reading rhythm. s0A gives the cleanest full table, while s0B gives a more useful first viewport. In the fitting class, both examples impose serious fragmentation; the main opportunity is to give the link and independence columns enough width for their repeated body values while preserving complete three-character codes.

analysis.strengths: The complete table is visible without horizontal scrolling, and the country names are mostly easy to recognize.
analysis.faults: Alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric codes split across lines, as do several headers. This damages the identifiers that readers need to look up and compare.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow code columns save width but force every row to be tall, leaving large empty areas beside fragmented content.

analysis.strengths: The wider alpha-2 column keeps its values intact, and the header is shorter than in s2B. The table fits the viewport.
analysis.faults: Many alpha-3 and numeric codes still split, and the headers remain heavily fragmented. ISO links require several lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: A small shift toward alpha-2 improves an important lookup field, but the fixed width still spreads the table over many tall rows.

analysis.strengths: Names, codes and links remain intact. Compact, uniform rows make scanning and comparison easy.
analysis.faults: The first viewport cuts through the numeric column and hides the link and independence columns. Reaching them requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Generous name width produces an exceptionally regular table, but it consumes space that could expose more of the code columns at first sight.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport shows the name and all three code columns in full. Identifiers remain intact, and most rows are compact.
analysis.faults: The long country name wraps, the first header occupies three lines, and the link and independence columns require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A modest reduction in name width buys a useful complete numeric column in the initial viewport, at the cost of one taller body row.

analysis.strengths: The alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric values stay together while the whole table fits the viewport.
analysis.faults: Several ISO links split their country suffixes, headers break inside words, and variable row heights make the table unusually long.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space is concentrated on the three lookup codes, shifting fragmentation and height into the link column.

rounds.insights: The fitted layouts cannot preserve every semantic unit at this font size and padding. Layout S protects the principal codes but sacrifices link readability and vertical rhythm; s2C is shorter but splits codes. Scrolling allows the identifiers to remain intact. Among the scrolling layouts, showing the complete numeric column initially is a useful trade for one wrapped country name.

bad.why: Splits several alpha-3 and numeric codes across lines, damaging the table's primary lookup task.
Splits repeated Yes values and fragments several headers, making the status column difficult to scan.
Splits repeated Yes values and breaks Independent into six lines without a compensating improvement in the body.
Splits numeric codes and repeated Yes values, while also fragmenting headers and some link identifiers.

contrast.why: Equal columns ignore the different lengths and roles of the content: country names and link identifiers would break severely, while short code columns receive space they do not need.

sameFunctionGroups.why: Both are short alphabetic country codes with parallel headings; matching widths support comparison, provided three-letter codes remain whole.
All three are lookup codes, but the numeric column needs enough width for its longer heading and three-digit values; identical widths are not essential.

synthesis.rationale: s0B keeps names and codes readable and shows the name plus all three code columns in the initial viewport; the remaining fields are available by scrolling. S is the strongest fitting candidate because its country codes and Yes/No values stay whole, although its headers and some link identifiers break awkwardly. S is a conditional finalist for the no-scroll requirement, not a satisfactory equivalent to the scrolling layout.

general: Protect complete identifiers and values used for lookup before optimizing table height or symmetry.
Judge a scrolling table both as a whole and at its initial viewport boundary.
Give parallel columns a consistent scale when their content and headings support it.
specific: At this viewport, showing all six columns forces serious breaks in at least the supplied fitting candidates.
The s0B viewport includes the country name and all three country-code columns, a useful initial view for this table.

synthesis.tradeoffs: s0B requires horizontal scrolling to reach the link and independence columns, and its longest country name wraps. Q reduces wrapping and gives a more even row rhythm, but its initial viewport cuts through the numeric column. S avoids horizontal scrolling at the cost of fragmented headers, broken link identifiers and much taller rows.
synthesis.uncertain: The fitting finalist is the least damaging of the supplied fitting candidates; a different allocation might improve it, but that would need a browser render. The relative value of Q depends on whether readers prioritize full country names over seeing numeric codes immediately.

critique.good: All six columns are visible at once, so the row relationships remain in view without scrolling.
critique.problems: Names, headers, alpha codes and numeric codes split within words or identifiers. The repeated three-line links make every data row tall, while the narrow columns create a fragmented, difficult-to-scan grid.
critique.cause: The 89px name column cannot hold some individual names; the 42px alpha columns and 48px numeric column cannot consistently hold their codes; the 69px link and status columns break their longer text.

critique.good: Names and codes are readable, most rows are compact, and the initial viewport shows the name and both alpha codes, with the numeric values also visible. The full table has a useful balance between width and density.
critique.problems: The alpha headers break after the hyphen, weakening the distinction between Alpha-2 and Alpha-3. Two links wrap, creating isolated taller rows. The numeric header is cut by the initial viewport edge, while the link and status require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 70px alpha columns are too narrow to keep the full header units together, and the 125px link column is slightly too narrow for every link. The first four columns total 387px, putting the viewport edge inside the numeric column.

critique.good: Every cell is on one line, with consistent row heights and intact identifiers. The full render is orderly and easy to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows the name and only part of the alpha-2 column; most reference values are off-screen. The width makes it harder to retain the country name while reading the rightmost fields.
critique.cause: The 282px name column and 118–121px code columns are sized for single-line headers, consuming substantial horizontal space that the short data values do not need.

critique.good: The initial viewport contains the names and all three code columns. Codes and links remain whole, and most rows have a consistent, compact height.
critique.problems: Both alpha headers break after the hyphen, making their identifiers harder to read. The tall header and the wrapped Antigua and Barbuda row interrupt an otherwise even rhythm. The link and status require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 70px alpha columns are too narrow to keep Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 together; the 138px name column forces the long name to wrap. The 155px link column preserves the links but contributes to the overall scroll width.

critique.good: All six columns are visible at once, so every row's fields can be seen without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Names, headers, codes and numeric values break within words or identifiers. The repeated three-line links make every body row tall, while the fragmented headers are difficult to scan. These breaks undermine accurate lookup and comparison.
critique.cause: The 44–48px code and status columns leave too little text space for their headers and some values. The 70px link column forces every link across three lines, and the 102px name column splits Afghanistan.

critique.good: The wider name column keeps all names on one line and produces a shorter header. Most links remain whole, and the full table is compact.
critique.problems: The alpha headers split at their hyphens. Two links wrap and make their rows taller, creating uneven space in the viewport without a visible explanation there. The numeric header is cut by the initial viewport edge, and links and status require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 70px alpha columns cannot hold their complete header identifiers. The 125px link column is slightly too narrow for some links, while the 165px name column pushes part of the numeric column beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Names and all three code values are visible together in the initial viewport. Codes and links remain intact, and the alpha columns have matching widths.
critique.problems: The name header takes three lines, and two country names create taller rows. Both alpha headers break after the hyphen, making the identifiers less immediately recognizable. The link and status require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 130px name column wraps American Samoa and Antigua and Barbuda; the 70px alpha columns break the headers at the hyphen. The 620px total width places the last two columns outside the viewport.

critique.good: All country names fit on one line, producing even body rows and a compact table. Codes, links and status are easy to read in the full view.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the numeric header and leaves the link and status offscreen. The alpha headers still break after the hyphen. The added name width makes the table noticeably wider to scroll.
critique.cause: The 165px name column and 76px alpha columns push the numeric column across the viewport edge; 76px still permits the alpha headers to break at the hyphen.

critique.good: All six columns are present in the viewport, and the numeric values remain whole.
critique.problems: Headers, some alpha-3 codes, links and Yes values split across lines. The resulting tall rows and fragmented text make lookup and comparison difficult, even though all columns are initially visible.
critique.cause: The 360px total leaves too little text width in most columns, particularly the 51px alpha-3, 61px link and 43px status columns.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows names and all three code columns together. American Samoa fits on one line, and the body is mostly regular. Codes and links remain intact.
critique.problems: Antigua and Barbuda wraps, the name header takes three lines, and the alpha headers break after the hyphen. Link and status lookup requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 138px name column is sufficient for American Samoa but not Antigua and Barbuda on one line; the 70px alpha columns encourage hyphen breaks. The last two columns lie beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Names and identifiers remain intact, the link is easy to scan, and nearly all rows have a compact, consistent height. The alpha headers retain their distinguishing labels.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the numeric header and leaves the link and status off screen. The alpha columns have more space than their short values need.
critique.cause: The first four widths total 384px; the 82px alpha columns push part of the numeric column beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All six columns are visible at once, and the short code values and status values generally remain whole.
critique.problems: Headers and links fragment into small pieces, making the columns difficult to identify and the links difficult to read. Link wrapping makes almost every row exceptionally tall and interrupts scanning.
critique.cause: The 48px link and status columns and 50–55px code columns leave too little room for their contents.

critique.good: The first viewport includes the name and all three code columns, with their values intact. The full table is compact, links and status are legible, and only the longest name needs an extra line.
critique.problems: Both alpha headers break after the hyphen, separating the distinguishing digit from Alpha. Link and status lookup still requires horizontal scrolling, at which point the name can move out of view.
critique.cause: The 70px alpha columns provide only 49px for text; the 628px total width exceeds the viewport.

critique.good: All columns are initially visible, and the wider link column reduces the extreme row heights seen in d1r3B.
critique.problems: Some alpha-3 values and Yes statuses split, undermining precise lookup. Headers are heavily fragmented, and links still occupy several lines in every row.
critique.cause: The 51px alpha-3 and 43px status columns are too narrow for their values, while 61px is still too narrow for a readable link identifier.

critique.good: Names and identifiers remain legible, the three code columns are visible together initially, and links remain on one line. The two wrapped names break naturally at spaces.
critique.problems: The alpha headers separate their digits from Alpha-, and the three-line name header is tall. Two taller body rows interrupt the otherwise regular rhythm. The link and status require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 74px alpha columns are too narrow to retain Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 together; the 130px name column wraps American Samoa and Antigua and Barbuda.

critique.good: All six columns are effectively visible at once, and the short alpha and numeric values remain recognizable.
critique.problems: Headers, links and even Yes fragment across lines. The resulting tall rows make scanning and matching values across a row laborious. The table also exceeds the stated 359px fitting limit.
critique.cause: The 45–57px non-name columns leave too little text width, especially the 52px link and 45px status columns. The 103px name column also forces several names to wrap.

critique.good: The full table is orderly and compact: all names, links and status values fit on one line, the headers have clear two-line breaks where needed, and rows have a consistent height.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the numeric column, so a reader cannot reliably see all three codes at first sight. Reaching the link and status requires substantial horizontal scrolling and moves the name out of view.
critique.cause: The 175px name column and two 82px alpha columns use most of the viewport before the numeric column begins; the full table is 689px wide.

critique.good: The initial view includes names and all three code columns. American Samoa fits on one line, Antigua and Barbuda wraps naturally, and links and status values remain whole.
critique.problems: Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 split at the hyphen in their headers, and the name header takes three lines. The link and status columns require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 70px alpha columns cannot keep the header identifiers together; the 138px name column is too narrow for the longest name on one line.

critique.good: All six columns are available without horizontal scrolling. Country names and three-digit numeric codes remain readable, and the consistent grid keeps each record together.
critique.problems: Alpha-3 codes and ISO identifiers split across lines, and several headers break inside words. Tall rows create large empty areas in the other columns, making comparison and continuous reading difficult.
critique.cause: The 45 px alpha-3 column and 54 px link column are too narrow for their values. The 45–61 px code and status columns also force disruptive header breaks.

critique.good: Country names and identifiers remain whole, with compact, uniform body rows. The first viewport shows names and both alpha codes, supporting common lookup tasks.
critique.problems: The viewport edge cuts through the numeric column, so its heading and values are only partially visible at first sight. The link and status require scrolling, and the wrapped header is taller than the body rows.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 320 px, leaving only 40 px of the 82 px numeric column visible. The 70 px alpha columns and 82 px numeric column wrap their headers.

critique.good: Every cell fits on one line, producing a calm, regular grid with clear headers and intact identifiers.
critique.problems: The first viewport shows the names and only part of the alpha-2 column; most comparison requires scrolling. Large spaces after short codes add width without helping the primary lookup task.
critique.cause: The 282 px name column and 118–121 px code columns are sized for one-line headers, making the table 907 px wide.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows the country names and all three code columns. Codes and ISO links remain whole, and most rows have a compact, consistent height.
critique.problems: The alpha headers break awkwardly after Alpha, Numeric splits inside the word, and Antigua and Barbuda makes one row taller. Link and status require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 65 px alpha columns and 75 px numeric column are too narrow for natural header breaks; the 154 px name column is too narrow for the longest displayed name on one line.

critique.good: All six columns are visible at once, and the numeric codes remain intact.
critique.problems: Alpha-3 codes, Yes, links and several headers split into fragments. The repeated tall rows make comparison slow and create a very long table.
critique.cause: The 46 px alpha-3, 73 px link and 42 px status columns leave too little text space. The 103 px name column also forces several names onto multiple lines.

critique.good: All displayed names, codes and links remain whole, with uniform body rows and natural two-line headers. The full table is orderly and compact vertically.
critique.problems: At first sight the numeric column is cut through, so its header and values cannot be read reliably without scrolling. Link and status are also offscreen.
critique.cause: The first three columns consume 320 px, leaving only about 39 px of the 82 px numeric column inside the viewport; the table totals 670 px.

critique.good: The first view contains the country names and all three code columns. Codes, links and status values remain whole, and the wrapped country name is easy to read.
critique.problems: The alpha headers break awkwardly before their hyphens, making the header taller and less clear. The link and status require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 66 px alpha columns are slightly too narrow for a more natural header break. The 145 px name column wraps Antigua and Barbuda, while the total width places the final two columns beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All columns are visible at once, most short codes remain whole, and the parallel alpha columns have equal widths.
critique.problems: The header is fragmented, Afghanistan and Antarctica split inside words, ABW breaks, and Yes splits throughout. Every link takes three lines, creating a very tall, repetitive table.
critique.cause: The 88 px name column is too narrow for some individual names; 54 px is insufficient for the widest alpha-3 value; the 42 px status column cannot hold Yes; and the 72 px link column forces repeated wrapping.

critique.good: All country names and identifiers stay on one line, the headers wrap naturally, and uniform row heights give the table a clear, compact rhythm.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the numeric column, so its values and heading cannot be read comfortably without scrolling. The link and status are also off-screen.
critique.cause: The 180 px name column and two 70 px alpha columns leave only about 40 px of the 82 px numeric column visible within the viewport.

critique.good: The wider name column keeps individual country-name words whole, and all six columns are present in the viewport.
critique.problems: Most alpha-3 codes split, undermining lookup and comparison. The alpha and numeric headers fragment, Yes splits, and the links make every row tall.
critique.cause: The 46 px alpha-3 column is too narrow for many three-letter codes; the 46 px alpha-2, 49 px numeric and 42 px status columns also force breaks in their headers or values. The 73 px link column produces three-line identifiers.

critique.good: The first viewport shows the country name and all three code columns. Identifiers remain intact, the alpha columns have matching widths, and nearly all rows are compact.
critique.problems: The country header takes three lines, and Antigua and Barbuda takes two. The link and independence columns require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 137 px country column favors showing all three code columns at first sight. The 155 px link and 112 px status columns preserve their content but extend beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All columns are nearly visible at once, and the short code and status values remain whole.
critique.problems: Headers fracture into difficult fragments, Afghanistan splits, and every link occupies three lines. The resulting tall rows make comparison and lookup laborious. The table also exceeds the viewport slightly.
critique.cause: The 98 px country column is too narrow for Afghanistan; the 45–58 px code columns and 46 px status column fragment headers. The 64 px link column drives the repeated three-line rows.

critique.good: Country names and body values stay on one line, producing a compact, orderly table with a shorter header than d2r3A.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the numeric column, making its header and values harder to read until the reader scrolls. Link and independence information are farther offscreen.
critique.cause: The 180 px country column preserves every displayed name on one line but pushes the numeric column across the viewport edge.

critique.good: The complete table fits the viewport, exposing every column at once.
critique.problems: Country names, headers, Yes, and the alpha-3 code ABW split inside words or identifiers. Three-line links make every body row tall, while the six-line header is especially difficult to scan.
critique.cause: The 88 px country column, 54 px alpha-3 column, and 42 px status column are too narrow for important values. The 72 px link column still forces three-line links.

critique.good: All columns fit in the viewport, country names remain recognizable, and the three code values are easy to compare across each row.
critique.problems: The fragmented headers are difficult to read, and several ISO links break inside their country-code suffixes. Uneven row heights make the table long and interrupt scanning.
critique.cause: The 45–55 px code columns and 46 px status column split header words; the 61 px link column is too narrow to keep link suffixes together.

critique.good: Names and identifiers remain whole, rows are compact, and the first viewport presents the country and all three primary codes together. The full table has a clear hierarchy and consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: The link and independence columns are entirely beyond the initial viewport, so consulting them requires horizontal scrolling. The link column has some spare width.
critique.cause: The first four columns use 359 px, while the 155 px link and 112 px status columns extend the table to 627 px.

critique.good: The link column keeps the country-code suffixes together, producing regular row heights and a shorter table than d2r4B. The code values remain legible.
critique.problems: Afghanistan splits across lines, header words fragment severely, and the links still break into three pieces. The table exceeds the viewport by 1 px, introducing scrolling without a meaningful gain in visibility.
critique.cause: The 98 px name column is below the width needed for the longest unbreakable country name; the 45–64 px remaining columns leave too little room for natural header and link breaks.

critique.good: All six fields are visible at once. The name column keeps most names readable, and the link and status columns are easy to locate.
critique.problems: Alphabetic and numeric codes break across lines, making identifiers difficult to read and compare. Header words fragment severely, and the repeated three-line links make the table very tall.
critique.cause: The three 40px code columns leave only 19px each for text. The 46px status column also splits its header, while the 90px link column cannot keep references together.

critique.good: Names and identifiers remain whole, the code columns are compact and comparable, and the first viewport shows the names and all three code values. Most rows have a consistent, compact height.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the numeric header and hides the link and status fields. The long first header and the wrapped Antigua and Barbuda row interrupt an otherwise compact rhythm.
critique.cause: The first four columns total 372px, placing the viewport edge inside the numeric column. The 150px name column requires the long name and header to wrap; the 155px link column uses substantial horizontal space.

critique.good: All body entries fit on one line, headers are mostly unbroken, and the rows form a calm, consistent reference grid.
critique.problems: The first viewport shows only the name, alpha-2 code and part of the alpha-3 column. The generous identifier columns spread related values apart and require considerably more scrolling to reach the remaining fields.
critique.cause: The 200px name column and 118px alpha columns prioritize single-line text over the compact body codes. Their combined width puts the viewport edge inside the alpha-3 column.

critique.good: All six fields are visible at once, and the name column keeps most names readable.
critique.problems: Several alpha-3 codes, status values and header words split across lines. Every subdivision reference breaks into three lines, making the table tall and difficult to scan.
critique.cause: The 50px alpha-3 column and 40px status column leave too little text space. The 66px link column forces references to wrap, while the narrow code columns fragment their headers.

critique.good: Names and identifiers stay whole, and the initial viewport shows the name and all three code columns. Most rows are compact.
critique.problems: The link and status require horizontal scrolling, which separates them from the name. American Samoa and Antigua and Barbuda each add a taller row.
critique.cause: The 135px name column wraps those two names; the 135px link and 112px status columns extend beyond the viewport.

critique.good: American Samoa fits on one line, only Antigua and Barbuda makes a taller row, and the link header and identifiers stay on one line.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the numeric header, and the link and status are further out of view. The extra link width produces a wider table.
critique.cause: The 150px name column pushes the 82px numeric column across the viewport edge; the 155px link column adds width beyond what is needed for the observed references.

critique.good: All six fields are visible at once, and the numeric codes remain intact. Most names remain readable.
critique.problems: The headers fragment severely, several alpha-3 codes and Yes values split, and subdivision references break across three or four lines. Tall rows make comparisons slow.
critique.cause: The 49–52 px code columns and 43 px status column leave too little text space; the 62 px link column forces identifiers to wrap repeatedly.

critique.good: Names and identifiers remain intact, nearly every body row is compact, and the initial viewport shows the name and all three code columns.
critique.problems: The alpha headers break awkwardly before their hyphenated suffixes. The link and status require horizontal scrolling, which can move the name out of view.
critique.cause: The 64 px alpha columns are too narrow for the more natural Alpha- line break. The 135 px link and 112 px status columns contribute to a 608 px table.

critique.good: All fields are visible together, and the numeric codes remain intact. The link column gives somewhat more coherent reference breaks than d3r2A.
critique.problems: Many alpha-3 codes and both status values split, while headers and links fragment. Uniformly tall rows create a dense, difficult reference table.
critique.cause: The 50 px alpha-3 column and 40 px status column are too narrow for their body values; the 66 px link column still cannot keep references together.

critique.good: Codes and links stay intact, the alpha headers break naturally after the hyphen, and the initial viewport shows the name alongside all three code columns.
critique.problems: American Samoa takes an extra line, and the link and status remain offscreen initially. The long horizontal span makes it harder to associate those fields with the name after scrolling.
critique.cause: The 135 px name column is too narrow for American Samoa on one line. The 135 px link and 112 px status columns increase the scroll distance.

critique.good: Names and the three code values remain readable, and the first viewport shows most fields.
critique.problems: The headers are fragmented, every subdivision reference takes three lines, and “Yes” breaks across two lines. The uniformly tall rows make lookup slow, yet the status still requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 53px numeric and 44px status columns are too narrow for their headers; 44px also splits “Yes.” The 83px link column wraps every reference.

critique.good: Names and code values are easy to scan, headers break naturally, and most rows are compact. The name column keeps American Samoa on one line.
critique.problems: Two subdivision references wrap, creating unexpectedly tall rows. The first viewport cuts through the numeric header, while the link and status columns are offscreen.
critique.cause: The 125px link column is slightly too narrow for the widest references. The first four columns total 372px, exceeding the viewport.

critique.good: All fields are present in the viewport, names retain whole words, and the alpha and numeric values remain intact.
critique.problems: Headers and “Yes” fragment severely. References break across four or five lines, sometimes splitting their final codes, and the resulting tall rows make comparison laborious.
critique.cause: The 53–55px code and link columns and 43px status column leave too little text width; in particular, the 55px link column drives row height.

critique.good: The first viewport shows names and all three code columns together. References and status are intact, headers break naturally, and the compact rows give the table a clear rhythm.
critique.problems: American Samoa and Antigua and Barbuda wrap, and the link and status require horizontal scrolling. The name can move out of view when consulting those later fields.
critique.cause: The 135px name column cannot hold every multiword name on one line. The 135px link and 112px status columns preserve their contents but extend the table beyond the viewport.

critique.good: All fields are visible at once, names keep whole words, and references generally take fewer lines than in d3r3C.
critique.problems: Several alpha-3 codes split, as do some reference suffixes and every “Yes.” Fragmented headers and tall rows make the table difficult to read and compare.
critique.cause: The 52px alpha-3 column is too narrow for some three-letter codes; the 62px link and 43px status columns also force breaks within values.

critique.good: The name and three code columns are visible together initially. Codes, links and status values remain intact, and only Antigua and Barbuda needs a second body line. The parallel code columns have a consistent scale.
critique.problems: The subdivision link and independence status require horizontal scrolling, and the country name can leave the viewport when the reader reaches them. The header is taller than most rows, though its breaks remain readable.
critique.cause: The first four widths total 367 px, while the full table is 615 px wide. The 145 px name column keeps American Samoa on one line; the 135 px link column preserves the references.

critique.good: All fields appear in the viewport, and the alpha codes remain intact.
critique.problems: Numeric codes and Yes values split across lines, as do many link suffixes and header words. The resulting tall rows make comparison slow and give the table an uneven, fragmented rhythm.
critique.cause: The 48 px numeric, 60 px link and 45 px status columns leave too little text space. The 46 px alpha-2 column also fragments its header.

critique.good: All fields are visible, alpha codes remain whole, and most links retain their suffixes on one line. Rows are generally shorter and more regular than in d3r4B.
critique.problems: Many numeric codes and Yes values split, some link suffixes split, and the six-line header is difficult to read.
critique.cause: The 48 px numeric and 42 px status columns are too narrow for their body values; 62 px for links is still insufficient for every suffix. The narrow identifier columns also force breaks within header words.

critique.good: The initial view shows names alongside all three code fields. Identifiers and status values remain intact, and the table has a clear, compact grid.
critique.problems: American Samoa takes two lines in addition to Antigua and Barbuda, making the table taller than d3r4A. Later fields require scrolling, which can separate them from the name.
critique.cause: The 135 px name column is 10 px narrower than in d3r4A. The 605 px total width places the link and status beyond the initial viewport.

critique.good: All fields are visible, numeric codes remain intact, and most links keep their suffixes together. The body rows have a relatively regular height.
critique.problems: Several alpha-3 codes and Yes values split, as do some link suffixes. Header words fragment heavily, weakening field identification.
critique.cause: The 52 px alpha-3 and 43 px status columns leave too little room for some body values. The 62 px link column cannot hold every suffix, and the compact code columns break header words.

d3r0A.idea: Fit all six columns within 359px, protecting body codes and most name words while accepting forced breaks in headers, links and potentially longer names.

d3r0B.idea: Use a compact scrolling table that keeps names and subdivision references readable while wrapping the longer headers.

d3r0C.idea: Use a spacious scrolling reference table with all headers and body entries on one line, favoring rapid scanning at the cost of more horizontal travel.

d2r0A.idea: Fit all six columns within 359px, giving the name the largest share while accepting forced breaks in headers, identifiers and some country names.

d2r0B.idea: Use a compact scrolling table that keeps codes and links whole, wraps longer names and headers naturally, and brings the three code columns near the initial viewport.

d2r0C.idea: Use a spacious scrolling reference layout with every shown cell on one line, prioritizing uninterrupted row scanning over the amount visible at first sight.

d1r0A.idea: Fit all columns within 359px, prioritizing names and links while accepting forced breaks in headers and some identifiers.

d1r0B.idea: Use moderate scrolling to preserve ordinary name wrapping, compact comparable code columns and a whole independence header.

d1r0C.idea: Use a wide scrolling reference table that accommodates the measured one-line headers and content, minimizing row-height variation and preserving identifiers.

d2r1A.idea: Test a more compact scrolling layout: fit the name and three code columns into the initial 359 px, while retaining whole code values and the full-width link and status columns. Some multiword names may wrap naturally.

d1r1A.idea: Test a compact scrolling layout: allow long multiword names to wrap, keep Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 intact, and widen the link column enough for all links on one line. The first four columns total 360px, bringing the three code columns into the initial viewport.

d2r1B.idea: Test a fitting layout that gives the link more room while preserving space for country names and numeric codes. Header and status-word splitting remains unavoidable; assess whether the wider link reduces row height and improves identifier reading.

d1r1B.idea: Test a fitting alternative that gives more space to names and alpha-3 codes while keeping all columns in view. It will still split some headers and links, so the render should be judged against the cost of scrolling.

d3r1A.idea: Test a fitted layout that gives the three code columns enough room for their body identifiers. The link and status headers will break more severely, but intact codes may improve the main comparison task.

d3r1B.idea: Test a more compact scrolling layout: the first four columns total 357px, bringing the three code fields into the initial viewport. Narrower name and link columns trade some natural wrapping for less scrolling while retaining room for whole identifiers.

d2r2A.idea: Try a scrolling layout that places the first four column boundaries within 359 px. The name column may wrap the longest name, but the numeric header and all three code fields should be visible initially.

d2r2B.idea: Try a fitted layout that gives both alpha columns more room, especially to preserve three-letter codes. This trades space from the name and link columns, so inspect the resulting name breaks and row heights.

d3r2A.idea: Try a fitted compromise that gives alpha-3 codes and status values more room while preserving the name column. The link and headers will still wrap heavily.

d3r2B.idea: Try the wider name column with narrower parallel alpha columns, keeping the first four columns within the initial viewport and retaining enough link width for the observed references.

d1r2A.idea: Keep the name and all three code columns within roughly the initial viewport while retaining whole links. Test whether a slightly narrower name column gives a useful viewport margin without causing disruptive additional wrapping.

d1r2B.idea: Prioritize a clean full-table reference: keep names and links on one line and give the alpha headers room to retain their identifiers. This requires more horizontal scrolling and places more of the numeric column beyond the initial viewport.

d1r2C.idea: Test a fitting layout that gives the three code columns more room to preserve values, accepting severe wrapping in the link and status columns. Compare whether improved code lookup justifies those compromises within 359px.

d3r3A.idea: Test a fitted layout that prioritizes intact alpha codes and shorter link wrapping. The widths sum to 403 px, so this is a compact scrolling alternative; the status header will still fragment.

d3r3B.idea: Combine the wider name column of d3r2B with the more natural alpha header breaks of d3r1B. Test a slightly narrower link column while preserving full references where their measured width permits.

d3r3C.idea: Test a 359 px fitted layout that gives the alpha-3 column more room to preserve three-letter codes, taking space from the link column. Links and headers will still wrap heavily.

d2r3A.idea: Test a scrolling compromise that places the first four columns at the viewport boundary. The 70 px alpha columns should improve their header breaks; the narrower name column will wrap some multiword names but should preserve individual words.

d2r3B.idea: Test a fitted layout that gives alpha-3 codes and Yes enough room while retaining space for country names and numeric codes. Accept more fragmented headers and link wrapping to protect the most important lookup values.

d1r3A.idea: Test wider alpha columns to keep Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 together in the headers while retaining the readable name and intact link columns. This increases scrolling and moves more of the numeric column beyond the initial viewport.

d1r3B.idea: Test a 359px fit that gives both alpha columns enough room for their body codes and gives Yes more room. The narrower link column will wrap identifiers more severely, so compare whether the improvement to code and status scanning justifies that cost.

d3r4A.idea: Test a modestly wider name column to keep American Samoa on one line while retaining intact references. The first viewport would cut slightly into the numeric column, so compare that cost against the shorter rows in d3r1B.

d3r4B.idea: Test a fitted compromise that gives alpha-3 codes more room and restores enough status width for “Yes,” taking space from alpha-2, numeric and link columns. Check whether all three-digit codes and reference suffixes remain intact.

d1r4A.idea: Test a scrolling layout that gives both alpha headers enough room to keep Alpha-2 and Alpha-3 together while keeping the first four columns at 360px. Names may wrap more often, but the principal identifiers remain together in the initial view.

d3r4C.idea: Test a fitted layout that prioritizes alpha-3 codes and subdivision references over the status column. It may retain the three-line reference pattern of d3r2A while reducing split alpha-3 values.

d1r4B.idea: Test a fitted layout that protects three-letter codes and Yes while retaining the minimum observed name width. The link and headers will still fragment, but the key row values should be easier to compare.

d1r4C.idea: Test a wider reference layout with more room for names and intact alpha headers. This favors continuous reading and fewer name wraps at the cost of more scrolling and fewer complete code columns in the initial viewport.

d2r4A.idea: Test a scrolling layout that gives country names slightly more room while keeping all three code columns within 359 px. Check whether the narrower parallel alpha headers remain readable.

d2r4B.idea: Test a viewport-fitting allocation that protects Afghanistan, three-character alpha codes, numeric codes, and Yes while accepting fragmented headers and wrapped links. The widths sum to 359 px.

d1r5A.idea: Test a scrolling layout that keeps the three code columns within the initial viewport while giving the alpha headers room to keep their identifiers together. Accept natural wrapping in more country names.

d1r5B.idea: Test whether the longest name fits on one line with less horizontal travel than d1r4C; retain compact alpha columns and compare the cost of their split headers.

d1r5C.idea: Test a 359px fitting layout that gives the link more room than d1r4B while retaining enough space for short codes and names. Header and status word breaks remain unavoidable; assess whether the shorter link wrapping improves the overall scan.

d3r5A.idea: Retain d3r4A as the scrolling reference: it preserves body identifiers and shows the name and three code fields together initially.

d2r5A.idea: Fit within 359 px while restoring enough name width for Afghanistan and giving the link column enough room to keep suffixes together. Balance the alpha columns more closely; test whether the narrower status column remains usable.

d3r5B.idea: Test a fitted layout that gives alpha-3 codes, numeric codes and Yes enough room to stay whole. The link column absorbs the reduction; its references will wrap more, but the primary lookup values should become easier to compare.

d2r5B.idea: Retain d2r3A's useful first viewport and intact country names and primary codes, while testing a narrower link column to reduce scrolling. The link header may wrap naturally.

d3r5C.idea: Test a narrower scrolling table while retaining the strong initial view and intact primary codes. Allow references to wrap at their natural space to reduce horizontal travel and bring status closer to the names.

s0A.idea: Combine Q's wider name column and single-line body rows with P's narrower alpha columns and R's narrower link column. This should reduce scrolling relative to Q while keeping identifiers whole; the numeric column will still be partly outside the initial viewport.

s0B.idea: Combine P's first-viewport access to the name and three code columns with R's narrower link column. This should retain P's lookup advantage while reducing total scroll distance, at the cost of a wrapped link header and long country name.

s0C.idea: For a fitted alternative, shift space from the alpha columns to the link column while retaining S's numeric and independence widths. This may reduce link fragmentation while keeping short values whole, but the tight alpha widths need a rendered check.

s1A.idea: P is already tested; instead, try a slightly wider name column while keeping the first four columns within the viewport: use the next design to explore the boundary.

s1B.idea: Give the name column a little more room while keeping the first four columns within 359 px. Check that both alpha headers and all codes remain intact and whether the name header improves.

s1C.idea: Fit within 359 px by moving width from the independence column to the link column. Test whether link suffixes stay together more often while Yes and No remain readable; the independence header will remain fragmented.

s2A.idea: Refine s0B so the first four columns total 359px, testing whether their complete headers and values fit within the initial viewport while retaining its natural alpha-header breaks.

s2B.idea: Test a fitting compromise that restores s1C's wider link column while keeping Yes and No whole as in S. The narrow code columns may fragment headers, so verify that all body codes remain intact.

s2C.idea: Test a second fitting balance with slightly more room for the Alpha-2 header and less for links; compare link wrapping and code legibility against the preceding proposal.

s3A.idea: Test whether two pixels moved from the yes/no column to the link column reduce split link suffixes while retaining intact alpha and numeric codes in a fitted layout.

s3B.idea: Test a more link-focused fitted compromise. The independence header will be narrower, but its short body values may still fit.

s3C.idea: Test a scrolling layout that places the boundary after the numeric column within 359 pixels while preserving the compact, readable structure of s0B.

contrast.idea: Equal columns ignore the different lengths and roles of the content: country names and link identifiers would break severely, while short code columns receive space they do not need.

s0B.why: Country names and codes are easy to scan, and the initial viewport contains the name and three code columns. The ISO link heading wraps naturally; its column and independence require scrolling.

d1r1A.why: The first viewport has the same useful coverage as A, and the ISO link heading stays on one line. The extra width slightly increases the distance to the independence column without changing the row heights.

contrast.why: Country names, headings and link identifiers fragment across many lines. The very tall header and rows make lookup laborious, despite the table being only one pixel wider than the viewport.

d3r4A.why: Names and codes scan cleanly, with compact, mostly uniform rows. The wider name column improves its heading break, but the numeric heading reaches the viewport edge and the last two columns require scrolling.

d2r4B.why: The country names and short codes remain mostly legible within the viewport, but headings split into fragments and ISO identifiers break over several lines, making rows tall and difficult to compare.

ref_equal.why: Equal narrow columns split country names, headings and identifiers repeatedly. The oversized header and tall rows severely hinder scanning, even though all columns fit.

ref_auto.why: Names and short codes are readable, but every ISO identifier wraps across three lines, making every row tall. The initial viewport also cuts through the link column, so it needs scrolling to read.

acceptance.unsure: B is the strongest scrolling layout by a small margin over A; A's narrower link column may be preferable if reducing scrolling matters more than keeping its heading on one line. E is the best fitting layout shown, though its fragmented headings and identifiers remain poor.

s0B.why: Names and codes are easy to scan, and the first four columns fit together in the initial view. The remaining columns require scrolling, and the wrapped headers make the header row tall.

d1r1A.why: The initial view keeps names and all three code columns together. The link header stays on one line, although its extra width adds scrolling without reducing the table's height.

d2r4B.why: All columns are visible and country names mostly remain whole, but headers break within words and link identifiers fragment across several lines. Tall rows make scanning slow.

d3r4A.why: Names and codes remain legible with compact, mostly uniform rows. The wider name column does not reduce wrapping in the body and leaves the numeric column edge beyond the initial viewport.

contrast.why: Equal columns split country names, headers and link identifiers repeatedly. The very tall header and rows make lookup laborious, while the table still exceeds the viewport slightly.

ref_equal.why: The table fits, but country names, headings and link identifiers break into fragments throughout. The towering header and sparse, tall rows severely hinder lookup and comparison.

ref_auto.why: Country names and short codes are readable, but every link identifier wraps across three lines, making every body row tall. The initial viewport cuts through the link column and hides the independence column.

acceptance.unsure: B is the strongest scrolling layout, though A is close: B's single-line link header costs 20 px of additional scrolling without changing row heights. C is the strongest fitting layout among those shown, but its broken headers and identifiers remain poor for publication.

d3r4A.why: Names and identifiers are intact, and the first view includes the name and three code columns. The first header leaves ‘case)’ isolated on its last line, and the final two columns require horizontal scrolling.

ref_equal.why: All columns fit, but country names, headings and link identifiers break repeatedly within words or codes. The extremely tall header and rows make scanning and lookup laborious.

d2r4B.why: Country names and short codes are mostly easy to find, but several headers fragment into small pieces and link identifiers split across three or four lines. Tall rows and scattered fragments impede comparison.

contrast.why: Like B, the equal narrow columns fragment country names, headings and link identifiers. The tall header and rows are difficult to scan, while the one-pixel overflow brings no meaningful reading benefit.

d1r1A.why: Names and identifiers stay intact, the link header fits on one line, and the first view includes the name and three code columns. The two rightmost columns require scrolling; the wider link column adds some horizontal travel.

s0B.why: The compact rows preserve names and identifiers, and the first view contains the name and three code columns. The link header wraps naturally, and the final two columns require scrolling.

ref_auto.why: Names and short codes remain legible, but each link identifier occupies three lines and makes every data row tall. The viewport cuts through the link column, while independence is offscreen.
